s2.verdict: The pull-back clearly reads as loss and abandonment: the boy starts large in the lane and is left smaller and isolated beneath the lanterns as the empty street widens around him. Both end frames are strong, the cut-outs remain coherent with no visible ghosting or tearing, and the subtle dust suits the 1950s offset-print treatment.
s2.rationale: A loss and turning point at his father's deathbed: the shot opens tight on the boy's back then pulls back as he shrinks, leaving him alone beneath the lanterns in the widening empty Chinatown lane.

s4.verdict: Publish. The pull-back clearly serves the loss in the story: it opens tight on the official bending over the fallen lifter, then visibly widens to the final full-hall dwell frame revealing the dropped barbell, silent paper crowd and hard overhead lights. Both first and last frames are strong still pictures that work in either direction, the light-sweep is subtle, and the 1950s offset-lithograph style is preserved. The plate itself has no stray text, no drawn faces where silhouettes/from-behind figures were directed, no anachronism, and no mangled anatomy or objects.
s4.rationale: Make the pull-back for loss decisive: open genuinely tight on the official bending over the fallen lifter, then widen through the platform to reveal the dropped barbell, silent paper crowd and hard overhead lights in the full hall for the dwell frame. Keep the official locked to the background lifter by using a background-near depth, no drift and no end-scale change, so the hand contact and feet o
filmIssues: Barbell's left plate touches the left frame edge in the opening frames, but it resolves cleanly as the pull-back reveals it — acceptable as part of the reveal rather than awkward clipping.
No visible tearing, doubling, halo or ghosting: the official remains locked to the fallen lifter at the hand contact and feet throughout, and the barbell stays coherent as a single foreground object.

s5.verdict: Judgement on both the film and the plate follows in the structured argument below.
s5.rationale: Make the triumph itself the movement: the locked-together lifter and barbell rise into full lockout in the first third (identical depth, drift, scale and rise entrance on both layers so the hand-to-bar join can never break), while the camera pushes in from the full arena and tilts its focus upward toward the bar and lamps. The slightly lower final zoom of 1.28 keeps the platform and feet inside th
filmIssues: The t=0 opening frame is an empty platform: the rise entrance hides the weightlifter and barbell, the subject of the scene, so the page opens without its hero.
Once the lifter appears the rise plus push-in does read as a triumph, and cut-1/cut-2 stay locked together with no visible tearing, doubled edges or ghost at the hand-to-bar join.
The final frame is a strong hold — lifter large, centred, bar overhead, platform and feet in frame — but the opening failure and the entrance pop keep it below publishable.
Light-sweep is fitting and subtle for the 1950s lithograph style, which is otherwise preserved.

s6.verdict: A sound pull-back idea for being singled out, undermined by an over-tight, clipped opening and a visible slice through the foreground figure; do not publish in this form.
s6.rationale: The turning point of being singled out for Rome is told as a reveal: the camera opens tight at zoom 1.38 on the handshake that seals the selection, then travels out to the full farewell table and bunting while the young man settles slightly under the weight of the responsibility.
filmIssues: The pull-back idea is legible, but the opening frame is awkwardly over-tight: at t=0-0.4 the young man's silhouette is clipped at the left and bottom edges and the bunting and headline bars are cropped, so the page does not open on a composed picture.

The foreground man shows a visible horizontal slice/tear at table height in the early frames, with his torso, extended arm and lower body misaligning across the table edge; the settle entrance plus strong parallax makes the cut-out read as separated from its painted-over spot.

Because the move is damped/clamped by the tight first framing, the handshake that is meant to be the reveal is not cleanly centred or readable — the hand sits at the table edge amid the slice, while the four officials remain small in the distance.
The final full-plate frame at t=1 is a good dwelling picture and the halftone-shimmer suits the 1950s lithograph style, but the faulty opening and tearing outweigh that.

s8.verdict: Good journey idea, but the visible halo around the lifter and the clipped spotlight in the final held frame keep it below publishable quality; the revised plan keeps the walk bold while easing the camera back.
s8.rationale: Make the journey, not the zoom, the story: open slightly left to include the watcher in the wings, then push in more moderately toward the platform while the lifter makes the maximum safe up-right drift toward the barbell and shrinks to 0.85, so he visibly travels away from the viewer into the spotlight. The barbell stays stable as the destination. The reduced final zoom and lower focus keep the m
filmIssues: The lifter's walk toward the barbell is legible, but a bright white halo / doubled edge is visible around his head and shoulders in every frame after t=0, betraying the cut-out as it moves off its painted-over spot.
The final push-in to 1.26 crops the top of the spotlight lamp and squeezes the red wing curtain at the left edge, so the held final frame is awkwardly clipped compared with the clean opening.
The journey is purposeful but partly undermined by the halo and by the excessive final zoom; the destination barbell is reached visually less by the lifter than by the camera.
